The contextual bandit problem in a non-stationary environment with random rewards has been extensively studied, but most research focuses on regret minimization through exploration. This paper takes a contrasting approach by utilizing Randomized Bonus Maximization Learning of the Exploration Probability to address the contextual bandit problem in a non-stationary environment with a possibly infinite action set. Our proposed framework, NeuralRBMLE, leverages a neural network to approximate the reward distribution's probability density function to determine exploration probabilities. This allows NeuralRBMLE to maintain a more accurate representation of uncertainty in rewards, thus providing a more informed exploration strategy compared to methods relying on uncertainty measures. Moreover, NeuralRBMLE adapts to non-stationarity through continuous learning and avoids the sub-optimality resulting from fixed exploration schemes. Our theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of NeuralRBMLE in addressing the contextual bandit problem in a non-stationary environment with a possibly infinite action set. To the best of our knowledge, NeuralRBMLE is the first model that applies the Randomized Bonus Maximization Learning of the Exploration Probability to address the non-stationary contextual bandit problem in a possibly infinite action setting. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharidev/NeuralRBMLE. We have also conducted a comprehensive experimental evaluation of NeuralRBMLE in a real-world setting, where we compared the performance of our model against other state-of-the-art algorithms in a real-world context. The code used in this evaluation is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharidev/NeuralRBMLE-real_world. The intra-halo light, comprising stars that are not found within galaxies, plays a crucial role in the integrated light of the galaxy and the large-scale background fluctuations of the universe. Utilizing the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we have conducted a statistical analysis of the intra-halo light within the SDSS-IV region, specifically focusing on the distribution of galaxies with varying magnitudes. By comparing the observed distributions of galaxies to those of the theoretical galaxy luminosity functions, we have identified the number of intra-halo stars, which are comprised of the difference between the observed and theoretical galaxy distributions. This difference, when corrected for the effects of galaxy luminosity, can be directly attributed to the intra-halo light. Our analysis has revealed that the intra-halo light constitutes approximately 8% of the total star population within the SDSS-IV region, with this value decreasing to less than 1% for galaxies of the highest mass. Furthermore, our results suggest that the intra-halo light is predominantly comprised of lower-luminosity stars, with a significant portion of the intra-halo stars belonging to the red sequence. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the intra-halo light is primarily composed of ancient stars, which have been ejected from galaxies through tidal interactions with the surrounding dark matter halo. Our analysis has also revealed that the intra-halo light within the SDSS-IV region is in line with the predictions of the semi-analytic galaxy evolution model, ROCKSTAR. However, our results suggest that the model may overestimate the intra-halo light within galaxy clusters. This discrepancy could potentially be attributed to the presence of an additional component of the intra-halo light, which is not accounted for by the model. This unaccounted component may comprise stars that have been stripped from galaxies through the process of galaxy harassment. This process is thought to be more effective within galaxy clusters than in galaxy groups. The current state of educational content is characterized by diverse formats like images, videos, and text, which present a complex problem for machine learning models. These models often struggle to effectively capture the underlying semantics of multimodal content, particularly when dealing with domain-specific domains such as education. In this study, we develop a comprehensive approach to uncover the underlying meaning of educational text-image pairs, utilizing a pre-trained cross-modal model to generate semantic representations. We then combine these representations with text-image relationships to create a new task, multimodal semantic matching, which enables us to identify and score the semantic similarity of educational content. To evaluate our approach, we introduce the EMCM dataset, a collection of educational text-image pairs, and conduct thorough experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method compared to existing state-of-the-art models. The results show that our approach significantly outperforms these models, achieving a substantial improvement of 10% to 15% in terms of accuracy. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately identifying visual metaphors across multiple datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art performance according to our standardized assessment metrics. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of our results to validate their reliability. Notably, our approach also exhibits versatility in handling other tasks, such as visual question answering and text-image retrieval, which further underscores its practical value. The prevalence of botnets poses a significant cybersecurity threat, with millions of devices compromised worldwide each year. By analyzing botnet communication patterns, cybersecurity experts can identify key indicators for detection and mitigation. However, current manual methods for analyzing botnet behavior are labor-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to human error. To address these limitations, this research proposes an automated approach that leverages natural language processing to identify crucial patterns in botnet communication. By analyzing the content of botnet messages, our model identifies significant features that distinguish them from regular network traffic. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by testing it on two real-world botnet datasets and achieving a high accuracy rate of 99% in distinguishing botnet and benign network traffic. Our findings suggest that this method has the potential to enhance cybersecurity measures, with implications for the development of more accurate anomaly detection systems. Additionally, our approach can be easily adapted to track emerging botnet variants in real-time, offering a valuable security advantage. We envision that this research can be further developed into a scalable cybersecurity platform for real-time botnet detection and tracking. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of CNNs in brain tumor segmentation. However, the performance of these models is often hindered by the absence of densely connected blocks. However, this analysis is often more complex when considering safety, which involves identifying situations where no future state violates a specified property. In this research, we develop an approach to verify safety in automata networks by translating the problem into a more manageable safety verification problem for individual automata, leveraging a technique to verify safety in automata networks through independent analysis of each component. Our proposed method is further validated by demonstrating its efficiency in solving a real-world problem - the verification of the TEGS protocol, a system used in the European e-Call emergency response system, through experiments. Our findings show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of time efficiency. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in verifying the safety of the TEGS protocol, which is not achievable using other existing tools. Our approach also provides a framework for verifying liveness properties in automata networks, enabling the verification of recurring sequences of states. In this research, a method is presented to transform visual data into RDF, which is then converted into a 64x64 grid of SPARQL triple patterns. The vast majority of existing research on named entities focuses on those that are explicitly mentioned, but neglects non-named and pronominal mentions, which are just as important.  To address this limitation, we have developed a novel entity typing framework that can identify the types of both explicit and implicit named entities.  Our approach is based on a neural network model that uses a shared vector space to represent all mentions, including both named and non-named entities, and a unique vector for each type.  To train the model, we utilize a combination of word embeddings and a neural network that combines the vectors of all mentions, for each type.  Our experimental results on a dataset of Wikipedia articles show that this approach achieves significantly better performance than a baseline model that is trained using only explicit named entities.  Furthermore, we have demonstrated that our model can be fine-tuned to improve its performance by incorporating pre-trained word embeddings for non-named and pronominal mentions, and that this can be done without requiring additional training data.  Our findings indicate that our entity typing framework is a promising starting point for developing more comprehensive models of entity typing that can accurately identify both explicit and implicit named and non-named entities. Mobile Augmented Reality applications are increasingly reliant on cloud-based services to deliver seamless user experiences, making efficient resource management crucial. A key strategy to optimize this management is service decomposition, which divides complex functions among multiple locations to minimize delays. However, conventional decomposition methods fail to account for the dynamic nature of mobile devices and their environments, resulting in suboptimal service placement. This paper introduces a novel framework that takes into account the mobility of devices and their surroundings when decomposing services, enabling more efficient service locations to be identified. The proposed framework utilizes machine learning techniques to model the potential delays associated with decomposed services, allowing it to determine the optimal placement of services based on the current device state and environment. The results of the framework's evaluation indicate that it significantly reduces the time it takes to locate optimal service placements, while achieving substantial end-to-end delay reductions compared to existing approaches. The proposed framework also demonstrates adaptability in diverse mobile scenerarios. The implementation of the framework is publicly available. A related patent has been filed. Multimodal learning has been proven to enhance performance in various tasks. However, traditional multimodal models are often limited to in-domain training and require task-specific fine-tuning for new domains. This paper proposes a multimodal model capable of adapting to new, unseen tasks with minimal fine-tuning data, thus enabling efficient transfer learning. Specifically, the model is applied to low-resource speech translation between European languages, where low-quality audio is used for training. This is achieved by pre-training a multimodal encoder on a broad range of multimodal tasks, including audio-visual translation, audio-to-text translation, and visual captioning. This pre-training process is then followed by a cross-lingual fine-tuning step, where the model is adapted to a specific target language using a small amount of data. Experimental results on the European speech translation dataset demonstrate the model's ability to achieve state-of-the-art performance in low-resource speech translation scenarios with minimal fine-tuning data, thus showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Furthermore, the model's source code and pre-trained models are made publicly available for research purposes. Source code is available at https://github.com/ritchiwei/low-resource-mt-adapter. This research tackles the long-standing issue of odometry drift in large-scale visual SLAM systems by introducing a novel loop closure detection approach. Our method leverages the geometric properties of 3D point clouds to identify loops, utilizing a deep learning-based model that maps these properties to a continuous space, allowing for flexible comparison and scoring. Unlike traditional methods, our approach does not rely on image features, making it more suitable for environments with limited visual variability, such as mines. We tested our method in two simulated scenarios and one real-world scenario, with the latter involving a mine navigation task. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in detecting loops and eliminating odometry drift. For future development, we provide insights into potential areas of improvement and suggest directions for feature extraction from point clouds. This paper addresses the multi-view detection issue, focusing on distinguishing between diverse object types. However, the limitations of space constraints and technological capabilities hinder the development of realistic haptic feedback systems. To address these challenges, we present a novel approach utilizing a compact, wearable haptic device to enhance teleoperated control of aerial robots within virtual environments. The proposed framework incorporates a high-frequency force controller, a real-time rendering algorithm, and adaptive compensation for the haptic system. Experimental results demonstrate the system's capability to replicate complex forces and interactions in a realistic manner, offering a more engaging teleoperation experience for users. The proposed method was evaluated in a series of studies where participants utilized the system to navigate a quadrotor to grasp and balance on moving surfaces. Notably, the introduction of haptic feedback led to a substantial 50% decrease in operation time, marking a significant breakthrough in teleoperated control of aerial robots. This work presents a groundbreaking approach to improving teleoperation of aerial robots, opening avenues for real-time haptic interaction in complex virtual environments. The developed framework is adaptable to various robotic systems and can be expanded to accommodate multiple degrees of freedom, paving the way for future advancements in teleoperation technology. This study presents an innovative approach to assessing the resilience of deep neural networks against input disruptions. By utilizing a pre-trained classifier, we generate a set of support vectors and evaluate the robustness of a network based on the number of classifier decisions that align with those of the pre-trained classifier when applied to various perturbed inputs. This metric, referred to as Robustness Ratio, effectively measures a model's capacity to withstand perturbations and can be easily applied to images, texts, and videos. Notably, our proposed metric demonstrates strong correlation with human evaluations and provides a comprehensive understanding of a model's robustness. Furthermore, our metric can be used to identify and rectify weak components within a network, enabling targeted improvements in its overall robustness. Experimental results on text and image datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach in evaluating deep neural network resilience. Additionally, our proposed metric can be employed to evaluate the resilience of video-language models in response to video perturbations, providing valuable insights into their performance. Lastly, our findings suggest that current robustness metrics fall short of human evaluations and that more comprehensive metrics are needed to accurately assess the resilience of deep neural networks. Robust optimization theories can be effectively applied to analyze structures subjected to uncertainty in loading by employing a robust formulation that incorporates loading uncertainty within the context of deformation structures. This paper presents a robust optimization framework that utilizes a set-based representation to account for uncertainty in both structural and loading parameters. The proposed method is grounded in a robust formulation that ensures the structural response remains within set-based limits despite variations in input parameters. The formulation is then reformulated into a mathematical programming problem with uncertain constraints, and a solution method is provided by approximating the robust constraint using a convex inner and outer approximation. The proposed approach is validated through numerical experiments and demonstrated to be effective in designing reliable structures subjected to variable loading conditions. The numerical results indicate that the proposed method yields reliable solutions that conform to set-based limits and consistently meet performance requirements. The proposed method is further demonstrated through an example application in topology optimization for a compliant structure subject to uncertain loading conditions. The numerical results show that the proposed method can effectively balance the design of compliant structures under uncertainty and achieve optimal performance. We examine how variations in the parameters of a network of oscillators affect the stability of synchronized groups. Initially, we find that when system parameters deviate slightly, group synchronization becomes unstable and instead the network experiences chaotic behavior. We then show that to maintain robust group synchronization under these conditions, the network's connections must be randomly distributed, with each node connected to at least a certain number of other nodes. By establishing this requirement, we prove that group synchronization remains stable even in the presence of small parameter variations. The findings are supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate the significance of the established connectivity constraint. Ultimately, our results highlight the importance of network connectivity in withstanding parameter variations in complex systems. We anticipate that these findings will contribute to the development of more resilient synchronized systems in various fields, such as power engineering, biology, and physics. By fine-tuning a pre-trained model with a single prompt, DPL achieves notable improvements in the performance of zero-shot CLIP on the GQA dataset, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. This paper presents a novel reverse engineering approach called reverse survival model (RSM) designed to enhance the transparency of deep survival models.  By assuming a patient's covariate profile and comparing the predicted risk of relapse with actual data points, RSM can pinpoint individuals whose survival patterns align with the model's predictions.  This method allows researchers to identify patients whose real-world outcomes are consistent with the model's predictions.  Experimental results demonstrate RSM's effectiveness in uncovering patterns within data sets, revealing patients whose survival patterns match the model's predictions.  Furthermore, RSM can be used to create a straightforward explanation of a deep survival model's decision-making process.  This paper presents a new method for explaining deep survival models and showcases its potential in medical research through case studies involving patients with kidney disease and those undergoing hemodialysis.  The results demonstrate RSM's ability to provide simple and understandable explanations for deep survival models.  This approach can be applied to other data-driven models beyond deep survival models, making it a versatile tool for researchers. Deep learning methods have been applied to clustering high-dimensional data, particularly with high-quality datasets, by training autoencoders to project data into lower-dimensional spaces for clustering. However, this approach can lead to unclear cluster boundaries and meanings due to the complex relationships between input data and cluster representations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel clustering algorithm that leverages autoencoders in conjunction with a clustering network and a clustering criterion function. The algorithm utilizes the autoencoder's latent space and the criterion function to identify cluster centers and assign cluster labels, while the clustering network helps determine cluster boundaries based on its predictions. These improvements enable the production of more interpretable clusters, as evidenced by experiments using the MNIST dataset. The findings indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of clustering quality. A thorough analysis is also conducted to examine the characteristics of cluster centers and their relationships with cluster labels. The complete implementation of our method will be made available to the public upon publication. The integration of renewable energy sources and advanced power grids creates complex challenges for energy system management, particularly with regards to balancing power production and consumption. To address this, High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) links can be used to effectively manage power flows over long distances, but their control mechanisms are limited by the single connection they provide. To overcome this limitation, new technologies like Multi-Terminal HVDC (MTDC) mesh interconnectors, and blockchain technology, can enable more efficient and autonomous control of power distribution within these networks. This paper proposes a novel control system for MTDC mesh interconnectors that utilizes blockchain technology, enabling decentralized optimization of power flows. Through simulations using a test network, the proposed system is demonstrated to effectively manage power distribution while ensuring power quality and reliability. Results show that this system can efficiently optimize power flows, balancing power generation and consumption, and can recover from potential power disruptions. Furthermore, the proposed system is shown to be robust against cyber-attacks, with simulations demonstrating its ability to detect and prevent manipulation of power flows. Overall, the proposed system is shown to be an effective solution for decentralized optimization of power distribution within MTDC mesh interconnectors. It offers a high degree of flexibility, robustness, and resilience in the face of power disruptions and cyber-attacks, making it a promising solution for future energy systems. Future work will focus on implementing this system in real-world energy systems. All simulation data and supporting code are available for review and evaluation. To facilitate this, the authors have made the following resources publicly available: (1) A blockchain-based MTDC simulator, (2) A blockchain implementation, (3) A blockchain transaction protocol, and (4) A blockchain-based MTDC simulation testbed. All resources are available for review and evaluation on GitHub. Finally, the authors highlight the potential for further research and exploration in this area, with a particular focus on the integration of blockchain technology in future energy systems. By leveraging blockchain technology, energy systems can become more transparent, efficient, and resilient, with a focus on the potential benefits and challenges of this emerging field. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the potential benefits and challenges of blockchain technology in energy systems. Deep learning models have become the gold standard for detecting anomalies in complex tabular data, but they often struggle with imbalanced data, particularly in real-world applications where anomalous instances are scarce. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that modifies the training process of anomaly detection models by prioritizing diverse learning experiences for both normal and anomalous instances. By introducing domain-aware mixup augmentations and a novel one-nearest-neighbor mixing strategy, we enable models to better recognize abnormal patterns and achieve more accurate and reliable results. Our experiments demonstrate that these algorithmic modifications significantly improve the detection performance of state-of-the-art models on real-world datasets. Moreover, we show that these enhancements enable the models to generalize better across different datasets and settings, resulting in more effective anomaly detection capabilities. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explore the benefits of modifying algorithms for anomaly detection in imbalanced data, particularly through domain-aware mixup operations. In machine translation, multilingual training enables a single translation model to learn multiple language pairs at once, leading to improved performance over individual models. However, this approach comes with a significant increase in training parameters, leading to a substantial memory footprint. This paper introduces a novel method called Gating Dropout, a form of regularization, to address this issue. By randomly disabling parameters during training, Gating Dropout reduces the model's parameter count without compromising performance. An additional mechanism involving gating networks and dropout determines which parameters to disable. Experimental results on machine translation demonstrate that Gating Dropout enables significant training speed increases of up to 2.5x, with minimal performance degradation, for both automatic and human evaluations. Moreover, this regularization technique can be applied to other NLP tasks, such as neural language modeling and document classification. Notably, this approach can be combined with other regularization methods to achieve improved results. Experiments on language modeling and document classification demonstrate that Gating Dropout can lead to improved performance when used in conjunction with other regularization techniques, leading to increased model speed and convergence. We also find that current approaches for selecting representative periods are inadequate, leading to inconsistencies in model outputs. Furthermore, we propose a new method, periodic optimization, to improve representation and output reliability. Our findings highlight the importance of effective period selection for capacity expansion models, providing insights for practitioners to select representative periods that accurately reflect the dynamics of energy systems. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of current approaches and suggest potential improvements to better represent energy systems in capacity expansion models. Our research aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the implications of period selection for low-carbon grid expansion modeling. A novel approach to enhance the interpretability of neural networks for fault diagnosis is introduced, leveraging formal language-based mechanisms. The proposed method integrates a neural network with a fault description module, which utilizes formal language to formalize the symptoms input by the user. This hybrid architecture, dubbed FaultDiagnosable, enables the incorporation of domain-specific knowledge to generate structured symptoms, improving interpretability by providing explicit symptom formulas and allowing for automatic rule-based inference. The network can also generate explanations for its predictions using the learned formalism, making it an effective tool for fault diagnosis in industrial processes. The performance of FaultDiagnosable is demonstrated through its application to a case study involving a three-tank system, showcasing its ability to accurately diagnose faults and provide transparent explanations. The comparison with other interpretable models reveals that FaultDiagnosable outperforms them in both fault diagnosis accuracy and explanation quality. The case study highlights the benefits of combining neural networks with formal languages in improving model interpretability and explainability. The corresponding code is openly available on GitHub for further reference. Our proposed algorithms are also efficient in terms of computational complexity, with a per-round complexity of O(n*2^l +m^2), where l is the depth of the model and n and m are the number of features and parameters, respectively. This makes our algorithms suitable for real-world applications. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on real-world datasets. Software developers are increasingly integrating user engagement measurements, such as measurements derived from A/B testing data, into their development processes. One approach to this is through the use of feature toggles, which allow for the separate analysis of system components without disrupting the overall software structure. However, there remains a lack of research on the impact of feature toggles on software evolution and maintenance. In this study, we investigate the use of feature toggles in 14 open-source projects hosted on GitHub, comparing the development pace and quality of these projects with equivalent projects not utilizing feature toggles. Our findings indicate that the adoption of feature toggles is associated with an increase in merge commits per branch, suggesting a higher level of development activity. However, this is not consistently reflected in the number of bug reports, which shows no significant difference in response to feature toggles. Interestingly, we also found that the overall complexity of the projects does not appear to be influenced by the use of feature toggles. However, this study does reveal a slight delay in the detection of bugs in projects using feature toggles, although this may be attributed to the increased activity levels in these projects rather than the feature toggle mechanism itself. Our results also suggest that the adoption of feature toggles may lead to a decrease in the frequency of code modifications, although this may be a positive factor for project maintainability. Overall, our study provides evidence of the benefits of using feature toggles in software development and maintenance. Nevertheless, further investigation into the long-term implications of feature toggles is necessary to fully understand their impact on software evolution. The behavior of the energy and magnetization of an Ising system with specific boundary conditions is studied. By removing specific edges from its perimeter, two distinct phases emerge. In one phase, the system's energy and magnetization exhibit a power law behavior with respect to the number of deleted edges. In the other phase, these properties exhibit a step-like behavior, with noticeable shifts in energy and magnetization at specific ratios of the number of deleted edges. This research aims to understand how the system's critical exponents relate to the high-dimensional system's volume and the number of deleted edges. By analyzing the system's phase diagram, it is discovered that the system's behavior approaches that of the standard Ising model when a certain number of edges is deleted. This deleted edge model can be used to explain the observed phase transitions in high-dimensional systems. By applying this model to a cubic lattice with periodic boundary conditions, it is possible to derive a phase diagram that matches experimental data for ferromagnetic phase transitions. This research demonstrates the potential of modifying a system's boundary to induce phase transitions in high-dimensional systems. It also highlights the possibility of using such phase transitions to develop novel computing architectures. This study introduces a novel deep learning-based framework, 4DVarnet, for estimating sea surface currents from satellite altimeter data. 4DVarnet utilizes four consecutive high-resolution altimeter measurements as input for a comprehensive analysis of the ocean surface's dynamic behavior. The framework's output is a detailed map of the surface velocity's temporal evolution, represented as a four-dimensional field. Through extensive testing on simulated data, 4DVarnet demonstrated superior performance compared to a standard recurrent neural network, particularly in capturing the complex patterns of the four-dimensional dataset. The results show that 4DVarnoised, a variant of 4DVarnet, achieved root mean square errors of 0.017 m/s and 0.012 m/s along with the mean dynamic topography, while the recurrent model yielded 0.026 m/s and 0.018 m/s. These findings highlight the significant benefits of incorporating temporal information through 4DVarnet in estimating sea surface currents. A fundamental problem in decision-making is to determine the optimal policy that maximizes the long-term reward. Traditional reinforcement learning methods view rewards as external motivators, assuming they accurately represent the desired behavior. However, rewards can be subjective and open to interpretation, requiring an understanding of their underlying meaning. Drawing from the concept of active inference, where rewards are seen as indicative of goal-directed behavior, we propose a new framework for policy optimization that avoids viewing rewards as external incentives. We demonstrate that this framework encompasses both reinforcement learning and active inference as special cases, and derive a novel algorithm that integrates the benefits of both without relying on distinct objective functions. We evaluate our algorithm on a complex task involving sequential decision-making and multi-agent interactions, finding it outperforms traditional methods in simulated environments. Moreover, we show that it effectively captures the underlying structure of human reward functions in a behavioral experiment. Our work suggests that integrating principles of active inference into reinforcement learning methods may lead to more effective and efficient algorithms for policy optimization. This paper introduces a novel, You Only Hear Once-inspired approach to audio event detection, which transforms audio signals into spectrograms and classifies them in a single pass. This method is significantly faster than traditional YOHO-based techniques, as it eliminates the need for frame-level classification. Instead, it uses a single, spectrogram-based pass to optimize speed, leveraging a range of network architectures, including 1D CNNs and 2D CNNs, to achieve this efficiency. Experimental results on the TUM Audio Event Detection System dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this accelerated approach, outperforming the current state of the art while achieving a substantial boost in speed, specifically 7.7 times faster. This improvement is further enhanced by the incorporation of a post-processing technique, resulting in an overall speed increase of 19.4 times faster than the current state of the art. This achievement marks the first time that the state of the art in audio event detection has been not only been surpassed but also significantly outdone in terms of speed, utilizing a single, spectrogram-based pass. This research highlights the potential of the YOHO approach in achieving a balance between accuracy and speed in audio event detection. This finding has significant implications for the study of open knot genus. Additionally, our research explores the behavior of the Jones polynomial for a specific type of open knot called torus knots and demonstrates that it approaches the value of $1$ when the parameter $t$ falls within a certain interval as the knot's endpoints approach each other. Moreover, our methods can be extended to a broader class of knots known as generalized torus links. The rapid expansion of automated summarization systems has led to a significant increase in the availability of high-quality summaries. However, the evaluation of these summaries remains a challenging task, especially with the growing number of human and machine summaries being produced. To address this issue, we present SummaryExplorer, an interactive data visualization tool designed to facilitate qualitative assessment and comparison of summary quality. By leveraging summary-paragraph-sentence relationships, SummaryExplorer enables users to identify and explore common and distinct features across different summaries. This includes enabling users to: (i) investigate how individual sentences contribute to their respective summaries, (ii) examine the overlap between sentences in summaries, and (iii) uncover unique features in summaries. Through user feedback, we found that SummaryExplorer effectively supports effective qualitative evaluation and comparison of automated summaries. Moreover, the tool allows users to gain deeper insights into the performance of summarization systems, ultimately contributing to their improvement. SummaryExplorer's implementation is web-based, open-source, and compatible with Linux, macOS, and Windows operating systems. It can be accessed at https://summaryexplorer.github.io/. We anticipate that SummaryExplorer will be a valuable resource for the NLP community to assess and advance automated summarization systems. We study a double well potential functional given by 
$F(u) = \frac{1}{2}(\|Du\|^2_a) + (1+z)^{p(a)}a^a$ in the domain
$\Omega \times \mathbb{R}$, where $\Omega$ is a bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
Given that $N \geq 2$, $p(a)$ is defined by the function $a^p(a) = 2a^2 + \log a$, and
$a_0$ and $a_1$ are positive constants, we observe that the functional's minimizer
exhibits a phase transition as $a$ approaches $a_1$ from below, switching from
a one-dimensional profile to a two-dimensional profile. This transition is
characterized by the value of $a_1$, which is approximately equal to $e^{4\pi}$.
Furthermore, we establish that the minimizer is Lipschitz continuous for $a < a_1$,
while for $a > a_1$, the minimizer is continuous but exhibits discontinuities.
Moreover, we derive a precise lower bound for the minimizer in the domain $a > a_1$. 
This research extends the findings of prior studies, specifically those of Abdulla and Tarulli for $N = 2$ and by Abdulla for $N = 3$. Our results are also applicable to the case of $p(a)$ being a linear function of $a$ and, in the process, provide an alternative derivation of certain bounds on the minimizer's behavior. These findings are not limited to the given functional and can be applied to similar scenarios with analogous outcomes. Additionally, we explore the implications of our results for related optimization problems involving the domain $\Omega$ and the role of $a_1$ in the context of such problems. Our research demonstrates that the value of $a_1$ is significant in the context of these optimization problems. Finally, we extend our results to the case of $p(a)$ being a non-linear function of $a$ and derive new findings for the given scenario.

The moment activation (MA) is a crucial parameter for understanding the behavior of a free-electron laser (FEL), as it is directly related to the coherent current in the storage ring. However, calculating MA is a complex task due to the presence of terms involving the product of the beam distribution function and the radiation field, which can be challenging to handle. Fortunately, a novel approach has been developed to efficiently compute MA by utilizing the fact that it can be expressed as a sum of products of functions, thereby allowing for the reuse of previously calculated values. Deep learning models have become increasingly prominent in various fields, but their deployment on edge devices is hindered by storage capacity limitations and computational inefficiencies. A potential solution lies in compressing model architectures to minimize storage needs and enhancing parallelization for faster inference times. This research introduces a novel approach to model compression, which involves decomposing convolutional layers into separate convolution and activation components and then applying a clipping mechanism to limit output values. By optimizing the clipped model, we can balance its accuracy with the computational constraints of edge devices. Furthermore, we develop a method for efficiently parallelizing the transformed models, which we test on a range of convolutional neural network models trained on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. The results demonstrate that our models achieve comparable accuracy to their full-sized counterparts while significantly reducing storage needs and computational times. Notably, we also observe substantial time savings for the transformed models, which can be further enhanced by leveraging the parallelization capabilities of modern GPUs. This research serves as a foundation for future studies exploring the application of our model transformation technique to more complex architectures and the deployment of compressed models on embedded devices. Human operators and autonomous systems collaborate to accomplish complex tasks despite their individual limitations. This research examines how trust is influenced by the success of an autonomous system in a dynamic environment. Specifically, we investigate the trust in an autonomous system that fails to complete a task when the operator is capable of completing it independently. A laboratory study was conducted, in which participants interacted with a robotic arm controlled by either a human or an autonomous system, and in various scenarios, the operator was able to successfully complete the task while the robot failed. Results show that when the robot fails, the operator exhibits reduced trust, and this decrease is more pronounced when the operator is capable of completing the task without the robot's assistance. Conversely, when the robot's performance is comparable to the operator's, the operator exhibits increased trust, and this increase is more pronounced when the robot's failure is attributed to environmental factors. These findings have implications for developing autonomous systems that can effectively collaborate with human operators. A model is proposed to explain the relationship between the robot's performance, the operator's capabilities, and trust. This research contributes to understanding the factors that influence operator trust in autonomous systems and provides insights for designing collaborative autonomous systems. However, training such models on multiple clients at once can be impractical due to the significant costs associated with communication. A more efficient solution, known as federated horizontal nesting (FedHN), allows for the training of models on multiple clients with shared features in a more cost-effective manner. Although previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of FedHN, its potential has yet to be fully explored. In this study, the feasibility of applying FedHN to training models on nested datasets with an increasingly wide range of tasks is demonstrated, as well as the effectiveness of extending FedHN to enable the training of models on interconnected datasets of varying sizes. These extensions enable the training of complex models on a wide variety of tasks with reduced communication costs. Our research also reveals that the proposed approaches outperform the baseline method, leading to significant reductions in communication costs, with our most advanced method reducing costs by up to 99.5% compared to the baseline. These findings demonstrate the potential of FedHN as a powerful tool for training machine learning models on a wide range of tasks with reduced communication costs. We introduce a novel framework for robotic trajectory generation through language, leveraging pre-trained language models as an encoding tool for user intent. These models are trained on vast amounts of unannotated data and incorporate intricate semantic and syntactic information. By harnessing them, we aim to enhance the effectiveness of language-based goal encoding in trajectory generation tasks. Initially, our framework employs the language model to produce an unstructured semantic embedding of the user input, which is then processed by a structured encoder – either a parser or a neural network – to achieve a semantically meaningful vector. Subsequently, this intent representation is combined with a grammar-based decoder to produce a feasible robotic motion plan. Experimental results on a KUKA Arm demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, yielding significantly improved trajectory quality when using a parser-based model. Additionally, our framework exhibits comparable performance to that of models trained on task-specific annotated data when utilizing a neural network-based model. Finally, our structured decoding component is shown to effectively leverage grammatical structure without compromising the model's generalizability. The impact of software vulnerabilities is a significant concern for various stakeholders, including project maintainers, developers, and decision-makers, who need to understand the consequences of these vulnerabilities. However, existing research lacks a systematic approach to assess the risk associated with vulnerabilities, neglecting to consider the relationships between projects and packages. This study proposes a novel method to quantify the risk posed by vulnerabilities to dependent projects and packages by analyzing network connections. We developed a comprehensive dataset of 1.2 million projects and 996,000 packages and their relationships, then applied our method to 2.5 million vulnerability-affected packages and their corresponding project and package connections. The results indicate that our approach is effective in identifying vulnerable projects and packages and can also rank projects and packages based on their exposure to specific vulnerabilities. Notably, our method can detect previously unseen vulnerabilities in unscanned projects and packages, underscoring its practical importance. Overall, this research underlines the significance of considering software project and package relationships when assessing the risk associated with vulnerabilities. We develop a model that links the quality of reform policymaking to the training and expertise of officials, and explore how governments can foster a culture of good policymaking. We find that central governments can play a crucial role in enhancing the quality of policy decision-making by offering training and support to subnational governments. algorithm ensures that the final policy meets the specified constraints, 
reaching an optimal solution if the constraints are non-diffuse. Importantly,

overestimation, making it a reliable method for constrained policy optimization.

We introduce a load balancing control method for a system with non-Poisson arrival patterns, utilizing local information from probing to make state-dependent decisions dynamically, whereas conventional methods rely on arrival rate assumptions. Our model incorporates two key components: (i) probe-driven control that utilizes real-time data from probing and (ii) stability analysis via the Loeb type Lyapunov function, which verifies the system's uniform stability regardless of non-linearities in the probe mechanism. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in outperforming conventional systems with non-linear queueing policies. Specifically, we show that our probe-driven method can effectively mitigate the negative impacts of non-Poisson arrival patterns on load balancing performance, even when the probing mechanism introduces non-linearities. This is further validated by simulations of queuing networks. Furthermore, we show that our approach can also enhance the performance of load balancing systems with non-linear queueing policies by incorporating the probing mechanism. Our results highlight the potential benefits of incorporating probe-driven control in systems with non-Poisson arrival patterns, even in scenarios where individual components exhibit non-linearities. This research also underscores the importance of considering the non-Poisson nature of arrival patterns when designing load balancing systems. Lastly, we emphasize the value of probe-driven control in systems with non-linear queueing policies. We provide a supplementary technical appendix for readers to replicate our numerical experiments. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of integrated end-to-end models for generating text, particularly the sequence-to-sequence auto-encoder paired with a pre-trained language model. Nonetheless, these integrated models are known to struggle with accurately capturing the meaning of input sentences, a concept referred to as semantic accuracy. In this research, we examine the impact of freezing the semantic parser component of the model during training on the semantic accuracy of the auto-encoder. We find that freezing the semantic parser enables the model to better replicate meaning in generated sentences compared to models that allow the semantic parser to train in parallel with the auto-encoder. We also discover that this improvement holds true across different input sentence structures. To further explore the semantic parser's role, we investigate whether the semantic parser is indeed capable of capturing meaning. We observe that when trained in isolation, the semantic parser fails to accurately interpret input sentences, suggesting that semantic parsing remains an unresolved challenge. Based on these findings, we recommend freezing the semantic parser during training for improved semantic accuracy in text generation models. We validate our results through human evaluations and provide recommendations for future work in semantic-parsed sequence-to-sequence models. We introduce C-DQN, a novel variant of the DQN algorithm, and apply it to a quantum cooling problem. The off-policy framework of DQN enables it to learn from diverse environments, but it often produces unstable policies due to sample bias. In the context of quantum cooling, a common issue is that the environment is influenced by the policy's parameter settings. To mitigate this, we propose a parameterization that separates the policy from its parameter settings, creating a consistent DQN model. The consistent model allows the agent to learn from diverse environments, but it may not always achieve the optimal reward due to the changing environment. In contrast, the C-DQN model incorporates a correlation filter that eliminates the correlation between the policy and its parameter settings, enabling the agent to learn from diverse environments and produce an optimal reward. As a result, the C-DQN model demonstrates greater stability and consistency than the traditional DQN approach. Furthermore, the C-DQN model's parameterization flexibility makes it suitable for a range of problems, and it can be easily adapted to various off-policy algorithms. The experimental results show that the C-DQN model outperforms the DQN approach in terms of stability and accuracy. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have the potential to efficiently process data by mimicking biological neurons, but they currently fall short of traditional deep learning models in terms of accuracy. A key factor contributing to this issue is the inherent noise present in the spike-and-dump process, where neurons fire randomly and the resulting spikes are discarded. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to mitigate this noise problem, leveraging the stochastic resonance effect in coupled oscillatory networks to extract meaningful information. We demonstrate that by connecting SNNs to these oscillatory networks, the resulting system exhibits enhanced robustness to spike noise, achieving a 50% reduction in accuracy drop for a given neuron density. Furthermore, we found that increasing neuron density also helps in mitigating the noise problem, resulting in a noise-resilient SNN that can be used in a variety of applications, including event detection in IoT and EEG analysis for emotion recognition. This framework's ability to distinguish between extrapolation and interpolation enables a more nuanced understanding of the models, providing a foundation for future research into the properties of extrapolation. Our approach offers a unified understanding of the asymptotic behavior of these polynomials as the degree approaches infinity, under conditions specified by the modified weights. The assessment of glacier health relies heavily on accurately segmenting glaciers in SAR images. However, current neural networks struggle to capture uncertainty, which can lead to over-optimism about their predictions. To address this limitation, we propose an uncertainty-aware glacier segmentation framework that integrates uncertainty into the segmentation process. By incorporating a new loss function and a U-shaped architecture, our framework produces more accurate glacier segmentations. In our experiments, we applied this framework to Sentinel-1 data from West Greenland, observing a significant improvement in glacier segmentation, particularly for smaller glacier bodies. Notably, our uncertainty-aware approach demonstrated a notable increase in accuracy compared to traditional deep learning methods. The resulting uncertainty maps also enabled the identification and removal of false positives in glacier predictions. Overall, our findings suggest that by incorporating uncertainty into neural networks, we can refine glacier segmentation and better understand the reliability of our predictions. This research delves into the geometric properties of a novel brush-stroke regularization technique. This method, inspired by high-dimensional painting, involves generating art by repeatedly drawing strokes on a low-dimensional canvas embedded within a higher-dimensional space. Our study centers on a key question: Given a set of points in high-dimensional space, how can we choose a subset of lines connecting them to form a low-distortion representation? We demonstrate that a representation consisting of a small number of lines, with minimal distortion, can be achieved, provided that a sufficiently large number of points are included. Our work also explores the implications of this finding for the problem of approximating low-distortion embeddings of metric spaces. An experimental component of the paper investigates the practical applications of the brush-stroke regularization technique in the context of data visualization. We present a prototype implementation of the related algorithm and apply it to the problem of visualizing large datasets. Our results indicate that a significant reduction in the number of points can be achieved, while maintaining the quality of the representation, through the application of the proposed regularization technique. We find that the level spacing variance can be an unreliable method for estimating the Thouless energy, especially near free fermion behavior. Instead, we suggest using the variance of the second-order R\'enyi entropy or the variance of the free fermion entropy, which are more consistent with the Thouless energy as the dimension increases indefinitely. Our analysis also reveals that the level spacing variance deviates from the Wigner-Dyson prediction near the free fermion limit, aligning more closely with the orthogonal or symplectic universality class as described by Wigner. Our results have implications for understanding SYK as a free fermion quantum spin chain in the large $N$ limit, which we verify by directly calculating the spectral statistics of the SYK model. Deep learning has greatly advanced the field of hyperspectral image (HSI) denoising, but existing methods are limited by their reliance on full spectral information, neglecting the complex relationships between spatial and spectral data across various bands. This paper introduces a novel spatial-spectral attention block (SSAB) that leverages the unique correlations between adjacent bands in HSI data. The proposed block incorporates a spatial attention module and a channel attention module to enhance the denoising process. The spatial attention module utilizes a convolutional layer to extract spatial features from each band, which are then combined with the original feature map through a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) block. The channel attention module applies a global average pooling and fully connected layer to obtain features for each band, and then uses a global average pooling and fully connected layer to calculate the importance weight for each channel. The proposed SSAB is integrated into a deep denoising network, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving the performance of existing deep models. The proposed method achieves superior results on various HSI datasets, including the Airborne hyperspectral image, hyperspectral WorldView-2, and hyperspectral data from the Indian Space and Climate Change Mission, with notable improvements in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). the mass spectrum and mixing patterns of scalar particles can be experimentally 
verified at the LHC. Meanwhile, the effects on the mass and decay patterns of 
tau leptons and bottom quarks are promising targets for testing at future 
colliders, such as the ILC and Belle II, with the added benefit of complementary 
tests at low energy scales. This review outlines the theoretical framework and 
the key predictions of the model, along with the potential experimental avenues. 
It also highlights the potential for Belle II to uncover the signature of CP-violating 
decays of tau leptons and Higgs bosons, such as the lepton-flavor-violating decay 
τ to μ. Furthermore, the model's implications for the muon g-2 anomaly and 
the constraints from lepton colliders are discussed. Additionally, the model's 
predictions for the properties of the Higgs boson, particularly its decays to 
leptons, are examined. Finally, the model's potential for explaining the observed 
baryon asymmetry of the universe is discussed. This review is part of a series

Electroweak Precision Tests, and Conclusion. The other parts of this series 
cover topics such as collider phenomenology, dark matter, neutrino physics, 
cosmology, and more. The papers are compiled in a single volume, available at arXiv.

This study examines the connection between healthcare access and general health in Germany, employing the Longitudinal Database for Statutory Health Insurance as its primary data source. We establish that individuals with health insurance experience improved routine checkups and general health and propose that insurance coverage serves as a mediator in this relationship. These oscillations give rise to a series of resonant peaks in the probability distribution, which are caused by the interaction between the oscillator and radiation. This research explores the capabilities of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in solving complex differential equations. We analyze the impact of increasing equations and time horizon length on PINNs' ability to learn the split function. We also evaluate the effect of model size on PINNs' performance and compare their results to a traditional neural network trained on the split function. Our findings indicate that PINNs can efficiently learn simple equations but struggle with more complex scenarios, ultimately limiting their potential in solving a wide range of differential equations. We discuss potential solutions to overcome these limitations. This study contributes to the growing body of research on PINNs and provides valuable insights into their capabilities. Our work is accompanied by a Python script that reproduces the research's results. We also investigate the potential of incorporating additional features to enhance the performance of PINNs, such as incorporating higher-order derivatives and multi-stage collocation methods. Our results show that this approach enables PINNs to learn complex equations more effectively. We believe that this work will be beneficial to researchers exploring the use of PINNs to solve differential equations. We also outline potential future research avenues in this field. Local quality adjustments involve dividing the video into smaller sections, applying distinct quality and bitrate settings to each, whereas efficient bitrate management involves identifying and minimizing unnecessary bitrate increases. These techniques are implemented using machine learning models trained on extensive video datasets. The results demonstrate that Gemino consistently outperforms optimized x264 and x265 codecs across various video sources and quality settings, making it a universal upgrade for legacy codecs. Moreover, the system's efficiency is demonstrated by its ability to process videos at a speed of 8 frames per second on a single core, accompanied by negligible additional latency. Bhojpuri, Magahi, and Maithili are North Indian languages prominent in daily life but face a significant resource gap in language technology development compared to Hindi. Although limited in tools such as morphological analyzers, these languages are essential for understanding online engagement and media consumption in the region. We address this gap by introducing a rule-based Bhojpuri, Magahi, Maithili and Hindi morphological analyzer, utilizing a hybrid approach that combines existing language technology and new morphological data. Our dataset, compiled from 40,000 unique words across four languages, is the largest available, with Maithili having the highest word coverage. Our four-language analyzer achieves 85.5% accuracy, with Maithili reaching 93.2% accuracy, making it the most accurate component. Our dataset and analyzer are made accessible through GitHub, enabling the development of language technology for these languages. Our work sets a new standard for developing morphological analyzers, with Maithili being the first Bhojpuri-related language to reach our accuracy benchmark. Our contribution aims to support further research in the field and stimulate the creation of language technology for underrepresented languages. We introduce an innovative approach to mapping the fermion subspace to the boson subspace, leveraging the fermion-boson transformation in a more efficient manner by exploiting the fermion Hubbard model's inherent symmetries. This results in a significantly more accurate representation of the Fermi liquid's low-energy properties, specifically in the self-energy and the Landau f-factor. Our proposed method is particularly well-suited for solving the Kohn-Luttinger problem, enabling a more precise analysis of collective excitations in both normal and superfluid states. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach can be adapted to various many-body problems beyond the Kohn-Luttinger problem, encompassing the Hubbard model and its spin and charge variants. Ultimately, we envision that our method will facilitate more precise ab initio calculations of collective excitations in both normal and superfluid states within the framework of the dynamical mean-field theory. This paper outlines a novel approach to designing Human-Computer Interaction through the lens of Optimal Feedback Control theory. Drawing parallels between users controlling devices and an aircraft navigating turbulent air, we've developed Fitts' T-joint model into a complex control system. Our goal is to create a framework that enables precise design of human-machine interfaces based on control theory principles. In addition to exploring the role of cognitive biases and task complexity, we propose using the Lyapunov exponent as a metric for evaluating task performance. A comprehensive case study examining the effects of human factors and task design on controlability and stability sets the stage for our theoretical framework's practical application. With the potential for real-time task evaluation, this approach offers a systematic method for designing and evaluating Human-Computer Interaction systems. Ultimately, we envision our framework as a valuable tool for designing and optimizing tasks for optimal performance and efficiency. The defect's spin relaxation is also affected by the distance from the vortex's core, with the closest and farthest distances resulting in the fastest and slowest relaxation rates, respectively. Recent advancements in video-language research have primarily relied on learning through proxy tasks, such as detecting actions, detecting objects, and answering questions. However, this research has led to a question of whether current state-of-the-art models truly comprehend the underlying text and visual data. To address this, we present a new framework called VICTOR, which enables video-language models to derive insights from visual data and text without the use of proxy tasks, effectively treating text and visual data as interconnected wholes. This novel approach is made possible through the incorporation of a visual transformer and text transformer, which are trained jointly to understand the underlying text and visual data through a process of self-supervised learning. Experimental results show that VICTOR achieves superior performance on a range of video-language benchmarks, outperforming current state-of-the-art models on tasks such as video question answering and visual grounding, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Our research focuses on utilizing saliency subitizing to generate more effective weak labels for salient object detection. Traditional approaches to this task rely on generating coarse masks through object localization, but these methods fail to accurately represent the complexity of salient objects. To address this limitation, we introduce a saliency subitizing module that enables the model to identify the number and locations of objects within an image. By incorporating object counts and center coordinates into the mask prediction process, our module produces more precise masks. Furthermore, to enhance model generalizability, we introduce a saliency subitizing loss function that encourages the model to predict object centers, object counts, and instance-level features. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Notably, our results show that saliency subitizing can significantly improve the performance of weakly-supervised salient object detection models.
